stories.bodyText:
India, among the world’s biggest economies, has also made significant strides in reducing poverty, especially extreme poverty in recent years. According to the latest World Bank report, India has managed to achieve one of the fastest poverty declines in the world - in both monetary and non-monetary dimensions.
Garibi hathao
 has been a slogan for decades, and now with extreme poverty falling from 27.1% to 2.6% between 2011 and 2023, the question is how far India has come in its fight against poverty, and how much further it still needs to go.
India’s remarkable poverty decline in numbers
How is poverty defined? Poverty in India, as well as in assessments by multilateral institutions, is measured with reference to specified poverty lines or thresholds.
Sharp Decline In Poverty Rate
The World Bank currently defines the international extreme poverty line at $3.00 per person per day in 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP) terms. According to the World Poverty Clock, extreme poverty may be considered eliminated when the poverty headcount ratio falls below 3%.
With the World Bank estimating India’s extreme poverty rate at about 2% in 2024, India can, on this measure, be considered to have crossed that threshold.
Between 2011 and 2023, the proportion of Indians living below the Lower Middle-Income Country poverty threshold of $4.20 a day (2021 PPP) dropped from 57.7% to 16.1%. 
This decline lifted an estimated 496 million people out of poverty. Over the same period, extreme poverty, measured against the $3-a-day threshold, fell from 27.1% to 2.6%.
Inequality falls
“Poverty is projected to continue declining, albeit more gradually, with the poverty rate at the $4.20/day line expected to fall from 14.2 per cent in 2026 to 12.1 per cent by 2028,” World Bank has said in its report.
Not just that, India has also recorded big improvements in non-monetary indicators of poverty. According to the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative’s (OPHI) Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), the poverty rate fell from 53.8% in 2005-06 to 16.4% in 2019-21. The World Bank’s MPI measure put the rate at 15.5% in 2022-23.
“As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment, and higher dependency ratios. Wage disparities, however, remain pronounced, as median earnings among the top 10 per cent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 per cent in 2023,” the report says.
How did India reduce poverty significantly?
The World Bank says progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. India's poverty reduction story is one of both convergence and concentration.
“Households in both rural and urban areas experienced substantial welfare gains, with faster progress in rural India significantly narrowing the rural-urban gap. Yet many of the households that remain poor continue to live in rural areas, where productivity is lower and access to higher-quality non-farm employment opportunities remain more limited,” the report says.
Poverty At Different Lines
Experts say the decline in poverty reflects a combination of income and employment growth, together with an extensive social protection system, including subsidised food provision and rural employment support.
DK Srivastava, Chief Policy Advisor, EY India says rural employment guarantee programme, earlier known as MGNREGA and presently referred to as VB-G-RAM-G, has also played an important role.
“India’s domestic approach to measuring poverty has traditionally used consumption thresholds consistent with minimum nutritional requirements and expenditure on specified non-food items. In 2011-12, the Rangarajan Committee re-estimated these poverty thresholds, with separate poverty lines for rural and urban areas and variations across states. These thresholds were substantially higher than the international extreme poverty line,” he explains.
Recent studies have updated the Rangarajan Committee-based poverty lines to 2022-23.
For example, a recent RBI study provides poverty estimates for 19 states using updated rural and urban poverty thresholds.
“On a population-weighted basis across these states, the poverty headcount ratio declined from 31.1% to 6.7% in rural areas and from 26.9% to 6.8% in urban areas,” he tells TOI, adding that several factors have contributed to this substantial decline.
Apart from broader income and employment growth, important policy interventions include the rural employment guarantee programme and the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY).
While Direct Benefit Transfer allows the government to transfer welfare benefits, subsidies and other payments directly to beneficiaries’ bank accounts, the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PM-GKAY) aims to provide free foodgrains to eligible households.
State governments have also implemented income-transfer and subsidy programmes targeted at lower-income households.
“The free food scheme has released resources for spending on other goods and services. Further, we have created new low paying but still income generating jobs in new sectors which have been booming like ecommerce, logistics and construction. This has added to income and spending power,” explains Madan Sabnavis, Chief economist, Bank of Baroda.
“Governments have paid attention to welfare which is needed at a time when the private system is unable to create jobs for all,” he adds.
Yet another major factor has been the accelerated capital expenditure by the government over the years.
Poverty By Group as per World Bank report
“This has been a significant contributor to impacting poverty. It has connected farms to markets and has led to better realisations for the farmers,” says Ranen Banerjee, Partner and Leader, Economic Advisory, PwC India.
Besides, it has allowed mobility of labour to urban areas for casual labour besides directly generating construction jobs.
Then, there are the multiplier effects of sectoral growth.
“The growth of the service sector and services exports have also created several organised sector jobs that has led to several multiples of unorganised sector jobs and this has also supported poverty alleviation,” Ranen Banerjee tells TOI.
Has this translated into a better standard of living?
Experts say there is little doubt that the standard of living has gone up.
“When free food is given, people have money to spend on other goods which would have otherwise gone for food. Similarly cash transfers and free travel have helped women to go out and work and led to better utilization of income. Therefore, there has been genuine improvement,” Madan Sabnavis tells TOI.
Changes in the composition of household consumption provide one indication that the decline in poverty has been accompanied by broader improvements in living standards.
DK Srivastava explains that one way to assess this is through the changing composition of private final consumption expenditure (PFCE).
Food, beverages and tobacco accounted for nearly 60% of total PFCE in the early 1960s; by the 2020s, their share had fallen to less than half.
At the same time, the share of non-food consumption has increased, including spending on transport, education, health, and miscellaneous goods and services.
“This shift from basic necessities towards a more diversified consumption basket is generally consistent with rising household incomes and improved living standards,” he says.
In fact, the structural shift has been particularly noticeable over the past two-and-a-half decades, from around 2000-01 onwards. While changes in consumption composition alone do not capture every dimension of household welfare, they provide supporting evidence that improvements in living standards have accompanied the measured decline in poverty.
Multidimensional Poverty Components
What’s the road ahead?
While the decline in poverty is an important achievement, as they famously say: one can't afford to rest on our laurels.
India, too, has a long road ahead.
The World Bank report also notes that poverty has also become increasingly concentrated geographically.
“While living standards improved across most states, households in a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal account for about 57 per cent of India’s poor population. As a result, further reductions in national poverty will increasingly depend on enabling productive employment in these states.” it says.
Poverty decline and growth in jobs are two different things. And the next phase of India’s poverty alleviation programme needs to be associated with economic growth that enables higher jobs and income.
Between 2017 and 2023, the number of employed people rose by approximately 134 million, which is nearly twice the increase in the working-age population.
A substantial part of this expansion has come from rural women entering paid employment, increasing the number of income earners within households, the World Bank reports says.
Labour market conditions have remained broadly resilient, with labour force participation and employment rates staying stable between the first quarters of FY2026 and FY2027.
However, the World Bank report notes that youth unemployment rose from 14.6 to 15.9 per cent between the two quarters, particularly among rural young women.
“Moreover, real earnings remained broadly unchanged with employment growth concentrated in relatively low-productivity activities,” it adds.
The catch is that government-backed programmes have been a big contributor to the decline in poverty. So the next question is, can governments keep doing what they are forever?
“If the food scheme is stopped, the Rs 2 lakh crore of subsidy will be withdrawn which means that people will slip down the income ladder. This is the major challenge of free cash/food. While they help a lot and can be accommodated in budgets, any cutback will risk making these people slip downwards. This is a challenge for us as we may not be having a skilled labour force in line with requirements of industry,” cautions Sabnavis.
Ranen Banerjee pitches for focus on spending on public health, skilling and education to support the households to come out of the poverty trap and get into gainful employment.
“The health insurance scheme is a very effective measure to prevent poorer households from falling back into the poverty trap owing to healthcare expenses derailing their upward mobility,” he tells TOI.
What’s important to understand is that India’s transition to upper-middle-income status will require sustained economic growth combined with higher labour-force participation, productivity improvements, technological absorption and continued investment in human capital.
The World Bank’s lower threshold for the upper-middle-income category is $4,636 per capita at market exchange rates for 2026-27.
India’s per capita GDP in 2026-27 is estimated at around $2,759 at market exchange rates and $12,998 in 2021 purchasing power parity terms.
Srivastava says that continuation of policies directed towards achieving developed-country status could enable India to cross the upper-middle-income threshold by the mid-2030s.
Three areas would be particularly important:
First, India would need to sustain real GDP growth of around 6-7% over an extended period.
Second, greater participation of women in productive employment could significantly expand the effective labour force and support household incomes and economic growth.
Third, India will need to manage the potential employment disruptions associated with rapid technological change, including artificial intelligence.
“This will require greater investment in research and development, faster adoption of technologies already available globally, and substantial investment in skilling and re-skilling the workforce. Together, these measures can help raise productivity and incomes while ensuring that technological progress translates into broad-based employment and income gains,” the EY expert tells TOI.
Robert Frost famously wrote, ‘miles to go before I sleep.’ To borrow from the poet, India still has miles to go before it is out of the woods on the poverty front.

briefs.headline: Mittal says India must hold satellite ‘kill switch’, warns against dependence on single provider
briefs.deck: Bharti Enterprises chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal says India should not rely on one country or company for satellite communications, as OneWeb, Jio and Starlink await operational clearances
briefs.bodyText:
Bharti Airtel founder and chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal has called for India to retain control over the “kill switch” for satellite communications operating in the country, warning against dependence on a single foreign provider as the government weighs security conditions for the launch of satellite broadband services.
“The kill switch, as we call it, should not be sitting somewhere else. India must have control over its own space destiny,” Mr. Mittal said in an interview with PTI marking the 50th anniversary of Bharti Enterprises.
His remarks come amid an increasingly public contest between satellite operators seeking access to India’s potentially vast market, with Elon Musk’s Starlink and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb awaiting regulatory clearances to begin commercial operations. The comments also come against the backdrop of a growing dispute over Starlink’s entry into India.
Mr. Mittal said OneWeb’s ground infrastructure had been ready for three years and its satellites had been orbiting over India for five years, but the company was still awaiting the government’s signal to begin commercial services.
The distinction between a satellite communications licence and operational approval is central to the contest. A licence does not automatically permit commercial operations. Spectrum assignment and compliance with security requirements remain necessary before services can be launched.
Three companies — Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, Reliance’s Jio Satellite Communications and Mr. Musk’s Starlink — have secured satellite communications licences in India. The government has maintained that operators must meet the same regulatory and security requirements, with final operational clearances dependent on compliance. Government sources have reiterated that the rules apply equally to all companies.
The national security question
For Mr. Mittal, however, the issue goes well beyond commercial competition and the allocation of spectrum. Satellite networks are increasingly becoming strategic infrastructure, with implications for national security, military communications and India’s ability to control critical data flows.
He pointed to the changing nature of warfare, arguing that satellites would play an increasingly central role in everything from drones and cyber operations to guided missiles.
“Whether it’s drones or it’s cyber issues, or indeed guided missiles and all, they’re all going to be managed from space,” he said. “Everybody in the world needs to have control over its security,” he added.
He said India would need appropriate safeguards and should not depend on a single country or company for critical communications infrastructure.
“Importantly, it may need to have different players. You can’t just depend on one country or one company,” Mr. Mittal said.
He said India must be able to monitor the equipment and communications coming down to the ground and ensure that “everything should be routed through India.”
The “kill switch” refers to the ability to disable, restrict or throttle satellite connectivity, whether for an individual terminal, a particular region or an entire network.
Satellite broadband relies on a combination of user terminals, satellites in orbit and ground infrastructure, including gateways that connect satellite traffic to terrestrial networks and the internet. Control over these systems can determine whether services remain available, how traffic is routed and who can intervene during a security emergency.
For governments, such control is an important instrument of national security and lawful oversight. But dependence on foreign-controlled systems can also create vulnerabilities, particularly during military conflicts or diplomatic tensions, when an operator’s decisions could affect connectivity on the ground.
Mr. Mittal cited Ukraine as an example of the growing strategic importance of satellite communications. “If Ukraine is using Starlink, it’s also using OneWeb now,” he said, referring to the use of satellite connectivity in the conflict.
The war has demonstrated how commercial satellite networks can become critical military infrastructure, supporting communications and battlefield operations. It has also highlighted the risks of relying on privately controlled systems whose service decisions can have consequences beyond commercial customers.
Mr. Mittal said the European Union’s efforts to develop secure communications infrastructure through Eutelsat OneWeb had also brought greater attention to the company. He cited European spending of around €14 billion to 15 billion on a secure communications network.
The Musk-Ambani spat
The regulatory contest has also become entangled in a public disagreement involving Mr. Musk and Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani. Mr. Musk recently accused powerful business interests of attempting to block Starlink’s entry into India and preserve what he described as a “monopolistic chokehold” on consumers. In posts on X, he referred to Mr. Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani,” questioning his influence over government decisions.
The Ministry of Communications had rejected suggestions that the regulatory framework or its application is discriminatory, describing such allegations as “baseless and misconceived.”
Reliance and SpaceX signed an agreement in 2025 to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian consumers through Jio’s retail network. Reliance is also developing its own satellite ambitions, including a proposed low-Earth-orbit constellation of around 1,600 satellites intended to extend connectivity to some 6 lakh villages.
Jio’s existing customer base of more than 524 million and its extensive distribution network give it a substantial presence in India’s digital market, while Starlink would need to establish its own customer base and operating infrastructure.
OneWeb awaits the signal
Despite the regulatory uncertainty, Mr. Mittal said OneWeb’s services were already technically operational and that the government had occasionally used its terminals for emergency communications.
He cited the example of economic adviser Sanjeev Sanyal, who took a OneWeb terminal on a boat trip to Oman and was able to stream throughout the journey. “He was streaming all the way through,” Mr. Mittal said.
“We were the first licence given by the government. We have satisfied all their needs, and we just now wait for their signal,” he said, expressing hope that OneWeb would receive the first commercial approval. He said the company was ready to activate services once the government gave the go-ahead.
On the contentious question of spectrum allocation, Mr. Mittal argued that satellite spectrum was inherently shared and required coordination between operators. “Everybody dips into the same spectrum,” he said, explaining that satellite operators at different orbital altitudes had to coordinate their use of frequencies. He said OneWeb had the highest priority in the Ku band, requiring other operators to coordinate with it, and added that regulators had understood the technical aspects of the debate.
Satellites to complement, not replace, mobile networks
Mr. Mittal also sought to temper expectations that satellite broadband would displace conventional mobile and fibre networks, arguing that satellite connectivity would remain complementary for the foreseeable future.
“It’s very expensive. Satellites need to be replaced every five, six years,” he said, pointing to the capital-intensive nature of building and maintaining satellite constellations.
“Where there is fibre, radio cannot compete with it. Where there is a radio, satellite cannot compete with it. But together all of them, just like radio and fibre coexist today, all three will coexist.”
The immediate opportunity, he said, lies in connecting areas where terrestrial infrastructure is difficult or uneconomical to deploy. There are still significant connectivity gaps in remote rural areas, forests, hills, mountains and maritime locations, as well as in aviation, he said.
Satellite services could provide connectivity to users in such locations, including people travelling through mountainous regions where conventional mobile signals are unavailable.
The broader significance for India is that satellite communications are increasingly being viewed not merely as another broadband technology, but as part of the country’s critical digital and strategic infrastructure. The challenge for policymakers will be to balance competition and investment with security, data sovereignty and operational control as global satellite operators seek access to the market.

briefs.headline: Stock markets snap three-day rally on rate hike fears; Sensex drops 318 points
briefs.deck: Retail inflation surged to 6.09% in October, breaching the RBI’s upper tolerance limit for the first time in two years and prompting expectations of a rate hike next month
briefs.bodyText:
Benchmark indices, the Sensex and the Nifty, ended lower on Friday (November 13, 2026), snapping a three-day rally amid expectations of a Reserve Bank of India (RBI) policy rate hike next month, after retail inflation surged to 6.09% in October.
The 30-share BSE Sensex dropped 318.56 points, or 0.39%, to settle at 81,592.45. During the day, it tumbled 622.26 points, or 0.75%, to 81,288.75. The 50-share NSE Nifty closed 155.05 points, or 0.61%, lower at 25,144.30. This is the first major decline for both benchmark indices this month.
Among the Sensex firms, Mahindra & Mahindra, UltraTech Cement, Bharat Electronics, NTPC, Trent and HDFC Bank were among the major laggards, while Hindustan Unilever, Asian Paints, Bharti Airtel and Reliance Industries were among the winners.
Retail inflation surged to 6.09% in October, breaching the RBI’s upper tolerance limit for the first time in two years and prompting economists to anticipate a policy rate hike by the central bank next month.
Consumer price index (CPI) based retail inflation had risen to 5.54% in September, and a sustained uptick in food and beverages, restaurant services and transport inflation played a key role in pushing up the October headline number. Data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation showed that food inflation spiked to 8.94% in October from 7.74% the previous month.
“The current correction suggests that markets are increasingly uncomfortable with the combination of elevated inflation, currency depreciation and rising crude prices. While global uncertainties are adding to the cautious sentiment, the bigger concern is the potential second-order impact of higher energy prices on corporate margins, consumption and India’s current account deficit,” said Vikram Kasat, Chief Business Officer, Advisory and Dealing, at PL Capital. With inflation moving beyond the RBI’s comfort band, expectations of monetary easing could also be pushed further out, limiting the scope for a sustained market recovery, he added.
“Indian equity markets closed lower on Friday, snapping their three-day winning streak as investors resorted to profit-booking following the recent extended rally. Sentiment was dented by October retail inflation surging to 6.09%, breaching the RBI’s upper tolerance limit and raising concerns over a potential repo rate hike in December,” said Ponmudi R., CEO of Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth-tech firm. On the macro front, crude oil and rising U.S. bond yields continued to weigh on domestic equities, he added.
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) bought equities worth ₹7,830.60 crore on Thursday (November 12, 2026), according to exchange data. In the broader market, the BSE MidCap Select index was up 0.09% and the SmallCap Select index 0.02%.
Among BSE sectoral indices, Realty dropped 1.70%, Auto 1.19%, Commodities 1.11%, Metal 0.93%, Oil and Gas 0.76%, Private Banks 0.68%, Insurance 0.67% and Bankex 0.64%. Telecommunication, Capital Goods, Power and Hospitals were the winners. A total of 2,462 stocks declined, while 1,965 advanced and 245 remained unchanged on the BSE.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, remained flat at $95.76 a barrel. In Asian markets, South Korea’s Kospi, Shanghai’s SSE Composite index and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index ended lower, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 settled in positive territory. Markets in Europe were trading marginally higher. U.S. equity markets ended lower on Thursday.
On Thursday, the Sensex advanced 31.61 points, or 0.04%, to settle at 81,911.01. The Nifty was up 44.30 points, or 0.18%, to end at 25,299.35.

briefs.headline: Copper prices slid to near four-month low amid fears of hike in U.S. interest rates, lower AI demand
briefs.deck: According to the industry body FIMI, prices are expected to remain volatile in the short-term though they may elevate in the long-term fuelled by increased demand.
briefs.bodyText:
Global benchmark prices of copper declined to a nearly four-month low Friday amid expectations of U.S. Fed increasing interest rates and lowered demand from industries, especially from China and the global technology industry.
At the time of writing, copper was trading about 1.8% lower than the previous day’s close at $13,461.99 per tonne.
“The recent fall in copper prices is mainly due to a stronger U.S. dollar, expectations of higher U.S. interest rates and concerns over weaker industrial demand, particularly from China,” industry body Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) told The Hindu.
Copper prices had gradually eased earlier this month following the results of the mid-term elections which gave a divided government to United States, thus assuaging concerns about tariff threats on refined copper imports – primarily responsible for the erstwhile rally.
“Profit booking by investors following the recent price rise and uncertainty over U.S. trade and tariff policies have also contributed to the decline,” the industry body further observed.
In addition to this, the recent Nvidia fallout has cast added apprehension about future investments in the realm of artificial intelligence and related technologies.
Further, the possibility of U.S. Fed hiking interest rates could increase the price of the metal – which is denominated in dollars – thus, bothering industrial activity and sentiment.
According to FIMI, copper prices are expected to remain volatile in the short-term.
“However, the long-term outlook remains positive due to rising demand from power infrastructure, renewable energy, electric vehicles and electronics, along with constraints in global mine supply,” it observed.
It added that lower prices would benefit copper-consuming industries by reducing import costs.
However, it cautioned a prolonged decline could discourage investments in domestic exploration and mining.
“We believe that India should continue to encourage domestic exploration, mining and processing to strengthen its copper supply security and reduce import dependence,” it held.

briefs.headline: 'Will be resolved very soon': India on Scotch imports from UK amid bulk shipments held at ports
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The government is hopeful of resolving the dispute over bulk Scotch whisky shipments held at Indian ports within the next few days, commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Friday.
Agrawal said product classification was among the key concerns being discussed and that the Department of Revenue was working to address the issue.
"Department of Revenue is working to resolve it. Classification is among the key issues. It should be resolved very soon...We are very hopeful that it would be resolved in some days," Agrawal said, ANI reported.
His remarks came after officials from the commerce and finance ministries met to discuss concerns raised by liquor companies over the classification of imported Scotch whisky.
Representatives of the International Spirits and Wine Association of India (ISWAI) and the Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies (CIABC) also met Agrawal to flag the differences over customs duties.
The dispute centres on whether bulk Scotch whisky imports qualify for the reduced 75% duty under the India-UK trade agreement, which came into effect in July, or should attract the 150% duty applicable to certain alcoholic preparations.
Customs investigators argue that the 75% tariff concession under the trade pact applies only to finished products, such as bottled Scotch whisky, and not to bulk concentrates that undergo further processing.
The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) has classified the imported goods as "compound alcoholic preparations", rather than finished whisky. This has led to a disagreement over the applicable Harmonised System (HS) code and the duty payable.
Earlier a confidential November 4 memo from the DRI, reviewed by Reuters, directed customs commissioners across the country to continue applying the higher duty.
It said importers were "incorrectly" claiming benefits under the India-UK trade pact for bulk Scotch shipments. The memo warned that any misclassification had "large-scale, recurring substantial revenue implications".
"Preliminary investigation revealed that the imported goods are not finished whisky/brand/rum as such, but are concentrated/compound preparations which are subjected to further manufacturing," the memo said.
The dispute has led to shipments belonging to several liquor companies being held at Indian ports.
Companies affected include Pernod Ricard India, Diageo, Radico Khaitan and Allied Blenders and Distillers, according to people familiar with the matter.
Pernod Ricard and Diageo each have more than 40 containers held at ports, while Bacardi has another five containers on hold, industry sources told Reuters.
The delays could disrupt supplies, the sources said. Tax officials have also searched the offices of several companies, including Pernod Ricard and Diageo, and questioned executives in recent weeks.
Around 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk and are subsequently used to manufacture Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL), which blends smaller quantities of Scotch with other spirits and ingredients.
Scotch whisky exports to India were worth $335 million in 2024. The Scotch Whisky Association has estimated that the India-UK trade agreement could increase the value of this trade by $1.34 billion over five years.
The International Spirits and Wines Association of India has cautioned that the dispute "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom".

stories.headline: IOA athletes’ panel ratifies SOM poll hours after vote, raises questions
stories.deck: The electoral process of the Indian Olympic Association for designating Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit has sparked significant concern. The Athletes' Commission hastily approved the election results, breaching the organisation's constitution. This raises questions about the validity of independent election rules versus constitutional mandates. Furthermore, reports of missing names on the…
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: In a curious development that has raised fresh questions over the Indian Olympic Association’s (IOA) electoral process, its Athletes’ Commission ratified the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) election results within hours of the polls on Nov 9, despite Article 3.7 of the IOA constitution stipulating that the eight SOMs be selected by the commission before their induction into the General Assembly.
Minutes of the virtual meeting, in possession of TOI, reveal that the commission recorded its “confirmation, adoption and ratification” of the independent election process after the results had already been declared. The meeting was held without any formal communication or circulated agenda, raising questions over the haste with which the exercise was endorsed.
The minutes themselves acknowledge that Article 3.7 provides for selection of eight SOMs by the Athletes’ Commission, followed by ratification by the General Assembly. However, the commission relied on the SOM Rules, which provide for an independent election through an 80-member roster. The question is whether these rules can override the constitutional provision, particularly when Article 32 states that the IOA constitution takes precedence over rules and bye-laws in case of a contradiction.
Olympic champion Abhinav Bindra had flagged precisely this inconsistency in a letter to IOA president P T Usha and CEO Raghuram Iyer, seeking clarity on the selection mechanism. 
The minutes now add another dimension: the commission ratified a process that had already been completed, instead of selecting the eight representatives beforehand.
The controversy is compounded by allegations of omissions from the electoral roster. Former international boxer Manoj Kumar, a Commonwealth Games gold medallist, told TOI that his name figured in the draft SOM list published on Oct 19 but disappeared from the final roster on Oct 23. He alleged a conspiracy to accommodate Dola Banerjee’s brother Rahul and said his complaints to the electoral officer, sports ministry and IOA went unanswered. Same happened with former international volleyball player Sukhpal Singh, whose name was initially included in the SOM roster but subsequently dropped.

stories.headline: Pakistan’s gritty Shakeel again misses out on a century in drawn test against Sri Lanka
stories.deck: Shakeel, who made 93 in Pakistan’s first innings of 434-9 declared, dug in for almost entire final day before he was bowled by Lahiru Kumara after facing 210 balls late on the fifth and final day
stories.bodyText:
Saud Shakeel missed out on a century for the second successive time but his gritty 97 foiled Sri Lanka's push for a win on the fifth and final day in the drawn first cricket test against Pakistan on Friday.
It was the first drawn game for Pakistan in its disappointing campaign in this World Test Championship cycle, losing seven and winning two of its previous nine test matches.
Shakeel, who made 93 in Pakistan's first innings of 434-9 declared, dug in for almost entire final day before he was bowled by Lahiru Kumara after facing 210 balls late on the fifth and final day.
By that time, the home team had reached 284-8 for an overall lead of 272 as the players shook hands and the match was called off.
Sri Lanka's pace bowlers had rattled the top order under overcast conditions in the first session by reducing Pakistan to 125-5, but Shakeel showed lot of temperament and shared a match-saving 92-run stand with Ghazi Ghori, who made 35, to deny Sri Lanka unlikely win.
Milan Rathnayake (3-47), Asitha Fernando (2-35) and Kumara (2-65) had given Sri Lanka a sniff before Shakeel stood firm and saved Pakistan from going down in the two-test series.
The second test will be played at the same Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium from next Tuesday after it was relocated to Rawalpindi due to increase in the smog level at Lahore.
Steely Shakeel stands firmPakistan's batters had stumbled against Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis' innovative field setting in the first session which was disrupted by 20-minute stoppage of play due to bad light.
Skipper Babar Azam scored 34 and Salman Ali Agha made 13 before both fell into Mendis' fielding trap and offered catches at short backward square leg on a second successive overcast morning at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium, where 117 overs were lost due to bad light and rain during the first four days.
Pakistan, which curtailed the Sri Lankan first-innings lead to 12 on the back of an inspiring seven-wicket debut by fast bowler Saqib Khan, led by just 139 runs at lunch and had given Sri Lanka a chance.
Shakeel successfully overturned an lbw decision against him early in the innings and also got a nasty blow on the shoulder off Dilshan Madushanka's short ball as the Sri Lankan seamers got plenty of seam movement in favorable conditions.
Resuming on 57-1, Pakistan had a disastrous start to the final day when both overnight batters, Azan Awais and Mohammad Taha, were dismissed without adding to their scores of 22 and 24, respectively.
Awais flashed hard at Kumara's first ball and was caught at slips while Fernando's delivery seamed enough to get the outside edge of Taha's bat from the other end.
Babar added 50 runs with the defiant Shakeel and struck six boundaries with his trademark cover drives and straight drives but yet again couldn't convert a good start into big innings as his century drought in test matches was extended to 42 innings.
Babar also survived two chances. Kamindu Mendis grassed a regulation chance in the second slip when Babar was on 22 and then had a close lbw call go in his favor on an umpire's call before he fell into Mendis' trap and gave a simple catch to Lahiru Udara.
Rathnayake executed the fielding plan well with another short ball to Agha and Pasindu Sooriyabandara brought up a spectacular catch before Shakeel and Ghori stood firm.

briefs.headline: 141 overs lost: Babar suggests 'pink' solution for Pakistan's winter Test problem
briefs.deck: The opening Test was repeatedly interrupted by bad light, forcing players to leave the field before the scheduled close of play on most days.
briefs.bodyText:
Pakistan head coach Mike Hesson has called for the use of the pink ball in day Test matches at home to be seriously considered after rain and poor light disrupted the opening Test against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi, which ended in a draw with nearly 141 overs lost.
Hesson and Pakistan captain 
Babar Azam
 are open to the idea of using the pink ball in future home Test series, particularly during the winter months when weather conditions make it difficult to complete scheduled playing hours.
The opening Test was repeatedly interrupted by bad light, forcing players to leave the field before the scheduled close of play on most days. The fourth day was called off during the afternoon session because of rain.
Even before the rain arrived on the fourth day, umpires had to suspend play because the light had deteriorated to a level where continuing with the red ball under lights could have put players at risk of injury.
The match was already heading towards a draw when play resumed on the fifth day. Pakistan were leading by just 45 runs with one wicket down as they looked to build a target for Sri Lanka.
Pakistan ended up batting through the day before play was called off at 4:18 pm, almost two hours before the scheduled close at 6:10 pm. 
The decision came after Saud Shakeel was dismissed in the 90s for the second time in the match.
The first three days had also seen significant interruptions, with only 14.2, 15.1 and 12 overs bowled in the evening sessions respectively.
The International Cricket Council (ICC), following its last quarterly meeting, has approved the use of pink balls in day Tests as an option to address the problem of overs being lost due to bad light. Hesson believes Pakistan should consider the option for future home series.
"It is certainly something that needs to be talked about for the future series," Hesson told the host broadcaster after the match. "It is going to be a challenge to play Test matches in this time of the year regardless of where in Pakistan. As the ICC have now allowed that to be an option, this is something that seriously needs to be considered before the series."
Babar, however, pointed out that the short gap between the two Tests would not have given Pakistan enough time to prepare for a pink-ball match. With only three days between the two games, he said players needed more time to get used to the different conditions and behaviour of the pink ball.
"You will need to prepare for it as we usually play with the red ball," he said in the post-match presentation. "A couple of days are not enough to prepare to play a Test with the pink ball. It is a good that we have it as an option, but the preparation for a pink ball Test demands more time."

briefs.headline: Matt Henry's three-ball demolition exposes India's batting frailties ahead of WC
briefs.deck: Matt Finishes India Off With Devastating 6/27, Including Wickets Of Rohit, Kohli & Iyer In Opening Over, As India Sink To Second-Biggest Defeat In ODIs; Will Young Sizzles With Ton In 244-Run Win For Kiwis
briefs.bodyText:
Three balls. That was all 
Matt Henry
 needed to turn India’s chase of 334 into a rout.
Henry was only supposed to be passing through. Having missed most of the T20Is with a leg injury and the early ODIs amid concussion concerns after colliding with Devon Conway, the seamer stayed back at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui simply to prove his fitness and get some overs into his legs before the Tests.
Instead, he produced one of the most devastating opening overs in ODI cricket, reducing India to 0/3 and setting up a 244-run thrashing — India’s second-biggest defeat by runs in the format. India collapsed for 89 and the contest was effectively sealed before the visitors had even troubled the scorers.
Henry’s first ball landed on a good length on off, kicked, and seamed away just enough to square up 
Rohit Sharma
 and kiss the outside edge on its way to first slip. It was a jarring sight, painfully reminiscent of the twilight of Rohit’s Test career and an increasingly familiar one when he faces quality fast bowling in overseas conditions.
Next up was 
Virat Kohli
. Henry pitched fuller, drew him forward and beat the outside edge by inches. Three balls later, he wobbled the seam from an identical spot. This one nipped back in, stayed low and rattled Kohli’s stumps.
Then came Shreyas Iyer, walking out for his captaincy debut and walking back with a golden duck — the first Indian skipper to suffer that fate. Trapped on the crease by one that darted past his inside edge, Iyer fell to a DRS review while Henry was already mid-celebration. 
India’s first run came off the 17th delivery of the innings.
For anyone watching, it was impossible not to be dragged back to Old Trafford in July 2019, when Henry’s 3/37 ripped the heart out of India’s World Cup semifinal chase. Seven years on, the scars remain wide open.
With the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa looming, where conditions could offer similar bounce and seam movement, this rout should set off alarm bells. A hint of lateral movement was all it took to expose India’s glaring technical chinks.
To be fair, Henry was not operating in isolation. Kyle Jamieson used his height to extract extra bounce and movement, getting Ruturaj Gaikwad (5) to edge a feeble push outside off to second slip as India slipped to 9 for 4.
Ishan Kishan (27 off 53) and Axar Patel (21 off 36) briefly resisted with a 44-run stand. Naman Dhir (21 off 24) muscled two sixes, but Matt Fisher (3 for 31) kept hitting hard lengths at high pace to snuff out any fight. Henry then returned to clean up the tail, finishing with career-best ODI figures.
If India’s batting was brittle, the thinking off the field was equally baffling. On a surface offering genuine seam and bounce, leaving Mohammed Siraj out of the XI again defied cricketing logic. Gautam Gambhir’s selection calls continue to puzzle, raising serious questions about the roadmap ahead.
Cruelly for India, they had walked into the innings break believing they held the momentum. After Tim Seifert (58 off 48) and Will Young forged an 85-run opening stand, Young took over and ensured there was no let-up.
Dropped twice on 5 off Auqib Nabi in the second over of New Zealand’s innings, Young cashed in with a career-best 125 off 108 balls. Alongside Finn Allen (41 off 30), he took down Kuldeep Yadav (0 for 73 in 8 overs) in a 90-run fourth-wicket stand before Rohit redeemed an earlier dropped chance with a sharp diving catch at short cover. 
Part-timer Naman Dhir then removed Young and took a diving catch to dismiss Michael Bracewell off Gurnoor Brar. Axar (2 for 39) and Arshdeep Singh, who removed Mitchell Santner, helped India take 6 for 77 in the final 13.1 overs and bowl New Zealand out for 333.
New Zealand, trailing 2-1, now head into Sunday’s final ODI without Henry and Jamieson, both bound for Test duty.

briefs.headline: One away from Zaheer! Kohli climbs to 2nd on unwanted list after NZ horror show
briefs.deck: In a challenging fourth ODI against New Zealand, Virat Kohli's recent dismissal led to his rise to 42 international ducks, placing him only one behind Zaheer Khan's 43. He also shares the dubious honor of having 20 ducks in ODIs with Sachin Tendulkar. India's batting collapse resulted in a heavy 244-run loss, making the upcoming final ODI essential for a turnaround.
briefs.bodyText:

 has climbed to second place on an unwanted list of Indian cricketers after his duck in the fourth ODI against New Zealand on Friday, moving closer to a record held by former India pacer 
Zaheer Khan

briefs.headline: Deepti Sharma named ICC Women’s Player of the Month for October
briefs.deck: Deepti Sharma beat Bangladesh’s Sobhana Mostary and Australia’s Annabel Sutherland to claim the monthly honour
briefs.bodyText:
India's star all-rounder Deepti Sharma was on Friday named the ICC Women's Player of the Month for October, winning the award for the second time in her career following a series of impressive performances against Zimbabwe.
The 29-year-old beat Bangladesh's Sobhana Mostary and Australia's Annabel Sutherland to claim the monthly honour.
"I'm pleased to win the ICC Women's Player of the Month award," Deepti said in an ICC release.
"The series against Zimbabwe was a great one for us, and I'm proud of the way the team performed, especially the youngsters.
"Scoring a century was a particularly special moment for me, made even more meaningful as it contributed to a winning cause."
Last year during this month, Deepti starred in India's World Cup triumph, and this year she showed fine form in the contests against Zimbabwe.
"I would like to thank the voting panel and fans for this recognition, as well as my teammates and coaches for their continued support," she said.
"I would like to dedicate this award to my fans across the world."
She yielded critical outputs across the two formats in Zimbabwe's inbound tour.
Deepti began with a quickfire 49 in the first T20I against Zimbabwe in Raipur to help setup a victory after the hosts were in a spot of bother at 19/4. Over the series, she collected two wickets to help India secure a clean sweep.
That form translated across to the ODI series as Deepti secured two wickets in the series opener in another India triumph.
This was followed by her standout performance in the second ODI, where the 29-year-old hit her second ODI century and chipped in with three valuable wickets as India clinched a 2-0 lead in the series.
In total, Deepti scored 155 runs and picked seven wickets across formats as India remained undefeated against Zimbabwe across the six international contests.
In men's cricket, South Africa all-rounder Marco Jansen was named the ICC Player of the Month for October after he played a pivotal role in his side's memorable 2-1 World Test Championship series triumph over Australia.
The 26-year-old overcame fellow nominees, Pakistan's rising all-rounder Arafat Minhas and West Indies' white-ball skipper Shai Hope to claim his first-ever Player of the Month accolade.

briefs.headline: Gambhir concerned about India's batting collapses ahead of World Cup
briefs.deck: “You’re always concerned when you get bundled out for 90-odd. Why won’t I be concerned? These are conditions which are going to be closest to what we might get during the World Cup,” Gambhir said
briefs.bodyText:
India getting bowled out for 89 against New Zealand in the fourth ODI here has left head coach Gautam Gambhir concerned as the collapse is not one off and happened in conditions that are similar to what the team will encounter during next year's World Cup in South Africa.
After India suffered a crushing 244-run loss to New Zealand here on Friday, Gambhir admitted that the manner and speed of the batting collapse, rather than the low total, was a worry ahead of the global event.
"You're always concerned when you get bundled out for 90-odd. Why won't I be concerned? These are conditions which are going to be closest to what we might get during the World Cup," Gambhir said at the post-match press conference.
"The bigger concern is not the runs. It's how quickly we got bundled out, around 26 or 27 overs. That is something which is always a concern," he added.
India had also struggled in the previous match, slipping to 111 for seven while chasing 135 in a rain-curtailed match, prompting Gambhir to underline the need for both technical and mental preparedness against the moving ball.
He said the first 10 overs in New Zealand are particularly challenging, unlike in India where the initial phase is generally the easiest period for batting.
"If you get 35 or 40 in the first 10 overs without losing a wicket, that is also good enough. Here, it's probably the most difficult time," he said.
Gambhir also said that India needed to be more decisive against the lengths employed by New Zealand pacers Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson, particularly the deliveries that left batters caught in two minds between going forward and playing off the back foot.
"I thought, more than the wobble seam, it's the areas that have probably created problems for us. It was that length where you couldn't go forward, you couldn't go back. It was that half-half length," he said.
Praising Henry's approach, Gambhir said the New Zealand pacer consistently attacked the stumps and challenged both edges of the bat, something the Indian bowling unit could learn from.
"He got Rohit in the slips and then got Virat and Shreyas beaten on the inside edge. That is something we need to learn, how consistently we can hit the stumps and keep hitting those pads as well," he said.
Gambhir also acknowledged that dropped catches proved costly, particularly the opportunities given to New Zealand centurion Will Young, who went on to make 125.
"He got those two chances and made the most of it. Things could have been a lot different, but there's always hindsight to what you do. We dropped catches, no one else did. So we had to pay for it," he said.
Defending the inexperienced Indian pace attack, Gambhir said the team had plenty to learn from playing in unfamiliar conditions but backed the young bowlers.
"I feel proud of everyone. Good days will pass, bad days will pass as well. There will be days like this, because this is what you learn from. Because the amount of inexperience you have in bowling attacks, it can be difficult as a captain and as a support staff as well. Because you're actually learning on the job.
"It's not like you've come into international cricket with no experience at all. So when you have so much inexperience, and when you come into alien conditions, but the way you've played in this one-day series, I think not only me, I think all of us should be proud of that.
He also explained the decision to play a wrist-spinner instead of Mohammed Siraj, saying the team felt a tweaker would be more useful on the bigger ground and provide an attacking option in the middle overs.
On the batting combination, Gambhir said India were trying to maintain continuity while giving players opportunities in different positions, adding that Ruturaj Gaikwad was preferred at the top because of his greater experience as an opener compared to Ishan Kishan.
Despite the heavy defeat, Gambhir backed the team to recover in the series decider, saying the players had enough experience and quality to bounce back.
"I'm sure the guys will turn up. It's important that they're hurting. I always believe that people should be hurting in the dressing room when you have this kind of a performance. If you're hurting, then obviously we can come back really strong," he said.

briefs.headline: Iyer claims nature of pitch changed from belter to seamer-friendly in heavy defeat
briefs.deck: “A tough one, I guess, to take that. There was a huge difference between the wickets between innings,” Shreyas Iyer, who is captaining India in ODIs for the first time, said during the post-match presentation
briefs.bodyText:
India skipper Shreyas Iyer on Friday blamed the change in the pitch for their massive 244-run defeat to New Zealand in the fourth ODI, saying it went from a belter to a seaming track.
He, however, vowed to draw inspiration from the first two ODIs, approach the next match with a fresh mind and level the series.
New Zealand posted 333 after being put in by stand-in captain Iyer, but India's batting line-up suffered a spectacular collapse, being bundled out for 89 in 26.4 overs. Pacer Matt Henry ripped through the top order to finish with figures of 6/27.
"A tough one, I guess, to take that. There was a huge difference between the wickets between innings," Iyer, who is captaining India in ODIs for the first time, said during the post-match presentation.
"But also credit where it's due, the way Henry bowled in the right areas right from ball one. I think that was sensational. We tried almost everything in the first innings, the way they were playing on the rise. And we thought that the wicket was better to bat on considering they got 330 after that. Obviously a couple of dropped catches, but that definitely happens in a game.
"But yeah, when we got into the dressing room, we thought that we would be cruising through the chase as well. But the way the ball was seaming in and out, you couldn't basically decide from inside that this is how I'm going to play. Or even if you saw the wickets, no one threw the wicket away. It was good deliveries."
The win kept New Zealand's hopes of levelling the series alive.
"It's important to forget about this one, obviously, analyze what went wrong in terms of bowling and batting. But at the back of the mind it's important that we have also won two games. So a lot of inspiration from that one and see to it that we come with a fresh set of mind," Iyer said.
New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner was pleased with his team's effort, though he felt they had initially fallen short of a competitive total by around 20 runs. The bowlers, led by Henry, made up for it by chipping away with wickets.
"Pretty happy. Didn't get to bowl again, so pretty happy. Young did his thing and we got a good score despite leaving a few out there. I think we were thinking 360, the intent was great. Maybe if we got 20 more each partnership, we could've gotten there but they chipped away with wickets," he said.
"Henry wanted to play today. With the new ball with a wicket that offers a bit, he's the best. Will chill tomorrow. Pacers will, I'll have to come and bowl. Then see what Sunday offers from a pitch and conditions point of view and take it from there."

briefs.headline: ‘They're a world-class outfit’: Matt Henry cautions against getting carried away after six-wicket haul against India
briefs.deck: Matt Henry said the sharp movement in the opening over put Indian batters under immediate pressure, particularly those facing their first deliveries
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand defeated India by a massive 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Mount Maunganui after bowling them out for just 89 while defending a target of 334.
Matt Henry starred with a sensational six-wicket haul, including three wickets in the opening over, which triggered India’s batting collapse.
Henry explained that his bowling strategy was to keep things simple, target the stumps and make the most of the new-ball conditions. He said the sharp movement in the opening over put Indian batters under immediate pressure, particularly those facing their first deliveries.
“Well, especially with the way the wind was going, I wasn’t too worried about the swing. So from ball one it was just about trying to have the strengths and bring the stumps in play, really. We knew that there was a small window there with the new ball that you could put the batters under pressure. So just trying to be as simple as possible, obviously, and when it moves sharply like that in the first over, when people are facing the first ball, it’s pretty tough,” Matt Henry said after the match.
Matt Henry (6/27) wreaked havoc on India’s top order, dismissing Rohit Sharma (0), Virat Kohli (0) and Shreyas Iyer (0) in a sensational opening over to leave the visitors reeling at 0/3. The Kiwi pacer returned to dismantle the lower order, removing Ishan Kishan, Kuldeep Yadav (1) and Gurnoor Brar (2) to register career-best ODI figures and bowl India out for just 89 in 26.4 overs.
Henry continued his impressive record against India in ODIs. The Kiwi pace spearhead has now claimed 27 wickets in 12 matches at an outstanding average of 17.33, including two five-wicket hauls.
Speaking on his impressive record against India in ODIs, Henry acknowledged Men in Blue’s world-class quality and cautioned against reading too much into one victory, stressing that the team would need to maintain its focus ahead of the next match.
“Oh, I don’t want to get too carried away. No, they’re a world-class outfit, and I think that’s the message that we were saying right through. They can bat deep, and yeah, look, it’s one game, and we’ve got another one coming up soon that hopefully we can level the series,” he added.
It proved to be a decisive result as the hosts trimmed India’s series lead to 2-1 heading into the final fixture on Sunday.

briefs.headline: Invictus again: South Africa’s cinematic rise to the Test summit
briefs.deck: The Proteas, under Temba Bavuma and Shukri Conrad, hold both the World Test Championship and the No. 1 ranking — a position of affairs that seemed unimaginable in 2024 when a second-string side, a compromise because of the SA20’s emergence, was thrashed by New Zealand.
briefs.bodyText:
Invictus must be one of the greatest films about sport. Because it is about much more than sport. It is about how Nelson Mandela saw the 1995 Rugby World Cup as an opportunity to unite a country where apartheid had only recently ended.
South Africa was hosting that World Cup. Mandela, the first black president of the country, was concerned that people of colour were not supporting the predominantly white Springboks ahead of the tournament. Morgan Freeman, one of the finest actors of our time, brought Mandela to life, while Matt Damon excelled as Springboks captain Francois Pienaar in the superbly crafted film directed by Clint Eastwood.
